Around 1450, a Venetian monk who had never himself travelled beyond the lagoon city of his birth produced what many historians consider the greatest geographical achievement of the medieval world. He worked in the monastery of San Michele on the island of Murano, assembling information from Portuguese sailors returning from Atlantic expeditions, from Arab geographic manuscripts, from accounts of Chinese maritime trade routes, and from merchants who had crossed the Eurasian continent.
The result was a circular map roughly two metres in diameter, drawn on vellum. It depicted Africa with its southernmost cape correctly rendered — implying circumnavigation was possible — nearly half a century before Vasco da Gama proved it. And unlike the Christian maps of his era, which placed Jerusalem at the centre and east at the top, his map — in deliberate acknowledgment of Islamic cartographic tradition — placed south at the top and oriented the world accordingly.
King Afonso V of Portugal, hungry for the geographic intelligence that would fuel his country's Age of Discovery, commissioned a copy in 1457. The original remains in Venice today.
Name this Venetian monk-cartographer, and what is his masterwork called?
